title: Mermaid Class Diagram Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: Class Diagrams in Mermaid
introduction.description: A class diagram is the blueprint of an object-oriented system, drawn before you write the code: which classes exist, what fields and methods each one has, and how they connect. Mermaid lets you write that diagram as plain text, and GitHub, VS Code (with a Mermaid extension) and mermaid.live turn it into a picture. Every example below uses the Employee system from the OOP lesson, and each one shows the source and the diagram it renders.

prerequisites: A place that renders Mermaid, e.g. a GitHub README/PR/issue, VS Code with a Mermaid preview extension, or mermaid.live
In a Markdown file the diagram goes inside a code fence tagged `mermaid`
Basic OOP vocabulary: class, field, method, `extends`, `implements`

steps.title: Start a Class Diagram
steps.description: Every diagram starts with the keyword `classDiagram`. A class is a box with three sections: the name on top, the fields in the middle and the methods at the bottom. Mermaid tells fields and methods apart by the parentheses - a member with `()` is a method.
steps.note: Constructors are listed with the methods, written like a method without a return type: `+ Employee(name, salary)`.

steps.title: Visibility Symbols
steps.description: A one-character prefix in front of a field or method says who may use it. It maps straight onto the Java access modifier.

rows: this class and all its subclasses

steps.note: In practice class diagrams almost only use `+` and `-`: private fields, public methods. `#` and `~` rarely show up in basic OOP diagrams.

steps.title: Fields, Methods and Types
steps.description: Write a field as `visibility name: Type` and a method as `visibility name(parameters) ReturnType`. Static and abstract members are marked with a symbol at the very end of the line.
steps.note: Pick one style for types and stay with it. This sheet uses `name: Type` for fields and a trailing return type for methods, as in the OOP lesson. Generics need the tilde because angle brackets would be read as part of the diagram syntax.

steps.title: Abstract Classes, Interfaces and Enums
steps.description: A label in double angle brackets as the first line inside the class box says what kind of type it is. Enum constants are listed one per line, with no types.

rows: cannot be instantiated; every subclass must fill in the abstract methods
a pure contract - defines what, not how
a fixed set of named constants

steps.note: An abstract method is marked with `*` at the end, so the label and the method together tell the whole story: the class is a template, and `onboard()` is the gap each subclass fills in.

steps.title: Relationship Arrows
steps.description: A line between two class names is a relationship, and the arrow style says which kind. The sections below explain how to choose between them.

rows: field; the parts are created outside and passed in
has-a (weak): the parts survive without the whole
field; the part is created inside the parent's constructor
owns (strong): the part cannot exist without the whole
passed as a method parameter, not stored

steps.note: The triangle of `<|--` and `<|..` points at the parent or the interface, so `Employee <|-- Manager` means Manager inherits from Employee. The diamond of `o--` and `*--` sits on the side of the whole. A solid line is a structural link, a dashed line is a looser one. Add a label after a colon: `Company o-- Employee : has`.

steps.title: Association, Aggregation or Composition?
steps.description: These three are easy to mix up. Ask three questions: is the other object stored as a field, who creates it, and can it exist alone?
steps.note: Rule of thumb: a permanent connection is a field, a temporary one is a parameter. The course material draws a parameter-only use as association (`-->`), while strict UML would call that a dependency (`..>`) - follow whichever your course or team uses, but be consistent.

steps.title: Inheritance: Abstract Class or Interface?
steps.description: Both are drawn with a triangle arrow, but the line style differs. Use the "is-a" test first: if "A is a B" is true, inheritance fits. A Manager is an Employee, but a Company is not an Employee, so that link is composition or aggregation.

rows: sharing code between closely related classes
defining a capability any class can have

steps.note: "Is-a" with shared code is an abstract class (`Circle` is a `Shape`). A "can-do" capability is an interface (`Manager` can be `Payable`).

steps.title: Multiplicity
steps.description: Multiplicity says how many objects of one class connect to how many of the other. Put it in double quotes next to the class it describes, one on each end: `Customer "1" --> "0..*" Order : places`. Read it left to right (one Customer places zero or more Orders) and right to left (each Order belongs to exactly one Customer).

rows: every Order belongs to exactly one Customer
an Order may or may not have a Payment
a Restaurant has at least one MenuItem
a Customer may have placed no orders yet

steps.note: Without multiplicity an arrow only says "these are connected". With it, the diagram answers real questions: can a customer have several orders, and can an order exist without a payment? Every value should come from a real rule in the system, not a guess.

steps.title: Putting It All Together
steps.description: The whole Employee Management System in one diagram: an abstract Employee with two subclasses, an enum, an interface with its implementation, and all three kinds of connection with multiplicities.
steps.note: Draw a diagram like this before you code. A missing class or a wrong arrow is cheap to fix on paper and expensive to fix in code.

gettingStarted.heading: Quick Syntax Reference
steps: `classDiagram` - the first line of every diagram
`$` at the end - static; `*` at the end - abstract
`List~Employee~` - generics use tildes, not angle brackets
`<<abstract>>`, `<<interface>>`, `<<enumeration>>` - the first line inside the class box
`A <|-- B` - B extends A; `A <|.. B` - B implements A
`A "1" --> "0..*" B : label` - multiplicities and a label
